messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Minh, a 31-year-old South Eastern Asian man who worked as a carpenter and lived with his wife, came to treatment after months of feeling as if his body had never really returned from the night police stopped him outside his apartment complex. He had been walking back from a late grocery run when officers ordered him to the ground, hands behind his head, and pressed him face-down against the pavement while bystanders watched. The shouting, the boots, the humiliation of being treated like someone dangerous when he knew he was only trying to get home, and the long minutes before anyone explained what was happening had left him frightened and enraged. What stayed with him most was not only the pain and fear in the moment, but the sense that at any time authority could turn on him again without warning, and since then he had lived with a constant readiness for danger that made ordinary life feel precarious.

Afterward, Minh found himself scanning every room before he could settle. He preferred to sit with his back against a wall so he could see who came and went, and even in his own house he felt uneasy if he could not watch the doorway or the windows. At work on construction sites, he became restless whenever a foreman was late, a delivery was delayed, or a customer took longer than expected to answer a question; his mind jumped immediately to the possibility that something bad had happened, or that trouble was about to break loose. Even when he was technically safe, he said he could not relax. His shoulders stayed tight, his breathing shallow, and he felt as if he were waiting for the next shoe to drop. That sense of danger kept him on guard and pulled him into the same attempts to manage it over and over: he would replay the incident in his head, blaming himself for not saying less, for not walking faster, for not somehow preventing the officers from losing control. He told himself he should have known better, that maybe he looked suspicious, that if he had been smarter or calmer none of it would have happened.

The more he noticed his body staying tense and his thoughts racing ahead to the worst, the more he tried to push the memory away. Minh stopped thinking about the stop on purpose whenever it started to rise into awareness, especially at night, but the effort rarely helped for long. He would open the garage, pick up a tool, or scroll on his phone to keep from going there mentally, yet the silence would eventually bring it back. When the memory broke through, he felt his pulse jump and the room narrow around him, which convinced him even more that he had to stay watchful. In turn, that watchfulness fed the rumination: the more he stayed keyed up, the more he revisited the scene and asked himself what he had done wrong, as if there were still some detail he could uncover to make the fear make sense. Drinking and taking drugs became part of that attempt to blunt the edge of it. On evenings after work, especially if he had spent the day on a job site feeling exposed or irritated by delays, he used substances to quiet the tension and to stop himself from thinking, but the relief was brief and left him more unsettled the next morning.

Over time, these habits began to shape his daily life. He was more withdrawn with his wife, less patient at work, and increasingly reluctant to go places where he might not be able to see everyone clearly. He arranged himself at restaurants, in waiting rooms, and in other people’s homes so he could keep his back to a wall, and if he could not do that he felt trapped. He noticed that the longer he spent trying not to think about the stop, the more easily the fear returned; and the more often the fear returned, the more he reached for self-blame and substances to settle it. The cycle had started to spill into the marriage, because his wife saw him as distant and tense, while he felt ashamed that he could not simply calm down. He finally sought help after an evening at home when a repair job ran later than planned and he became convinced, without evidence, that something awful must have happened to the client. He realized how exhausting it had become to live braced for danger and to keep trying to outrun his own thoughts. What he most wanted was to feel safe enough to sit in a room without guarding every exit, and what frightened him most was that if he did not get help, the police stop would keep controlling the rest of his life.
